wheel.bolt_pattern: 5x150 (1999 facelift on); earlier trucks use 6-stud wheels

max_tire.note: IH8MUD consensus for a stock long-wheelbase 70. 285/75R16 goes on but rubs inside at full lock on factory steel wheels unless the wheel offset changes; sagging old springs make everything rub sooner.

timeline.change: 70 Series replaces the 40 as the heavy-duty Land Cruiser: short, medium and long wheelbases, leaf springs front and rear
BJ70 sold in small numbers in Canada (3B, later 13B-T); diesels switch from 12 V to 24 V for the 1986 model year
4.2 L 1HZ diesel straight-six arrives (HZJ7x) and stays in production for decades in less-regulated markets
Second facelift: coil-sprung live front axle, longer rear leaf springs, 5-stud wheels; pickup becomes the 79, Troop Carrier the 78; short wheelbase dropped in most markets
Japanese sales end in June because the 70 can't meet Japan's NOx and particulate law

Big facelift for the 4.5 L 1VD-FTV turbo-diesel V8: wider front track and chassis, flat front fenders gone, 76 four-door wagon and GXL grade added. Unsealed 4X4 says many enthusiasts favour the 2007–16 V8s, which are simpler because they have no DPF
4.0 L 1GR-FE V6 replaces the 1FZ in petrol markets
Double-cab HZJ79 pickup added on the long 3,180 mm wheelbase
Limited '30th Anniversary' GRJ76 wagon and GRJ79 double cab return to Japan for one year (V6, 5-speed manual)

From late 2016 (Euro 5), the V8 gets a diesel particulate filter and piezo injectors; the single-cab ute gains curtain and knee airbags and a stronger chassis for a five-star ANCAP rating. The DPF is the most-discussed fault on later V8s
2.8 L 1GD-FTV four-cylinder with 6-speed automatic added alongside the manuals; LED headlights, 40-Series-style gauges. The 70 returns to Japanese showrooms in November
Australian V8 wagon, Troop Carrier and GX utes end production in September; GXL V8 utes continue to late 2025. A 5-speed manual 2.8 arrives in October

identify.intro: The '70' badge covers forty years of engines, wheelbases and body styles, and the US never sold one new. Every truck here is a gray import, so make sure the code on the paperwork matches the metal.

items.head: Model code = engine + wheelbase
items.body: The prefix letters name the engine: FJ = 3F petrol, FZJ = 1FZ petrol, BJ = 3B diesel, HJ = 2H, HZJ = 1HZ, PZJ = 1PZ, LJ = 2L family, KZJ = 1KZ, VDJ = 1VD-FTV V8, GRJ = 1GR V6, GDJ = 1GD. The numbers give the body: 70/71 short wheelbase, 73/74 medium, 75/78/79 long (pickup and Troop Carrier), 76/77 four-door semi-long wagons.

items.head: Pre- or post-1999
items.body: From the August 1999 facelift, trucks have a coil-sprung front axle and 5-stud wheels. Earlier trucks have leaf springs at the front and 6-stud wheels. The three-bar grille with upturned ends also dates from that facelift.

items.head: Not every '70' is a heavy-duty 70
items.body: From 1985 to 1996, Toyota also sold lighter-duty models under the 70 designation, called Bundera, Land Cruiser II and later Prado. They grew into the separate 90-series Prado, so don't pay heavy-duty money for one.

items.head: V8 front clip
items.body: 2007-on V8 trucks lose the flat front fenders and get a wider front track and chassis. If a 'VDJ' still has the old flat-fender nose, look harder.

items.head: Lockers
items.body: Selectable front and rear diff locks were factory options in some markets, not standard everywhere. Confirm working factory lockers rather than trusting the ad.

values.intro: Every US truck is a 25-year gray import, so condition and paperwork drive the price. Diesel Troop Carriers and clean, low-kilometre 79 pickups bring the most.
values.note: Based on 17 Bring a Trailer sales, April–October 2026, from a $13,250 1992 LJ77 to a $55,600 27,000-km 1999 HZJ79 double cab. HZJ75 Troopies sold for $29k–42k.

paragraphs: Toyota never sold the 70 Series new in the United States. Canada got small numbers of BJ70s for the 1985–87 model years, and later trucks only through Toyota Industrial Sales for the mining industry. Every US 70 is a gray import.

Since 1989, NHTSA has exempted vehicles over 25 years old from its rules, so the window rolls forward each year. That's why US auction results are full of 1980s and 1990s FJ, BJ, LJ, HZJ and FZJ trucks, and why late-1990s and 2000-ish HZJ79s and HZJ76s now appear. California's smog rules make registering an overseas classic difficult there even when the federal 25-year rule is met, so check your state's titling and emissions rules before you buy.

production.intro: Production began in 1984 and continues today: one of the longest runs of any Toyota.
